content:
I signed a $5k/month lease with only $10K left in my bank account. That decision made me almost over $500k in 12 months.

Comfort is the most dangerous place you can be as an entrepreneur. When things are fine, your brain goes quiet.

I already had a business, but I wasn't paying myself yet. Living in a small room at my friend's place. Not the right environment for creativity to flourish.

So I put a deadline. 30 days. $10K in the bank. $5,200 due on the first.

Two weeks later, I came up with Outliers - my "online frat" for successful young founders.

Seven-figure minimum to get in. $5K to join.

1.5 years later: 100+ members, all doing 7-9 figures annually. $15k to join, probably raising it soon. The youngest just sold his company for high eight figures at 18.

Most people will never find their best idea. Not because they're not smart enough, but because they never got uncomfortable enough to need it.

When you're desperate, you get creative. When you're comfortable, you get complacent.

Stop waiting for the right conditions. Sign the lease.

content:
I borrowed $250K from my employee at the beginning of this year.

When he first joined the team, he worked for free for 6 months when I couldn't afford him. I gave him 2% equity as a thank you.

Now he's betting on us again.

Here's why this matters:

We're scaling from $9M to $60M+ this year. I owed $3 million on inventory but the traditional lenders like Shopify and WayFlyer wanted basically 30% APR after all their interest and fees.

So I texted my friends: "Anyone want to loan me money? I'll give you 15% interest."

One person said yes. The same guy who worked for free when I was broke because he believed in what we were building.

Now he's investing again. Not just for the return. Because he knows we're going to win.

When I first met him, his skill exceeded my bank balance. So he worked for free and I gave him 2% equity for that leap of faith.

Those are the people you want to build with. The ones who throw it down when things get hard.

Your cap table should be full of believers. Your lenders should be people who want you to win.

When you're growing faster than your bank account, you find out who's really on your team.

Build with believers, not just employees.

I got cheated on in college, and I deserved it. 

That experience taught me the most valuable business skill I have.

In college I was president of the house. Everyone knew my name. I thought my status made me bulletproof.

When she cheated, my first reaction wasn't heartbreak. It was ego: "How could she do that to ME?"

Looking back, I wasn't present. I was too busy being "the man" to actually be a good and present boyfriend.

That lesson followed me into business. I've trusted relationships over structures and got burned every time.

The skill that breakup taught me: saying "I was wrong."

Most young guys think admitting fault makes you look weak. It's the opposite.

Your ego doesn't protect your business. Accountability does.

content:
Kids in college these days will never know how good they have it. There has never been more opportunity than ever before for them to make money. 

Would you rather work as a bouncer as the local bar making $15 / hour or make TikTok Shop and Trybe videos and over $1k / day. 

You can pay your way through a full 4 year degree by just making a few videos a day (about products and brands you actually like).

There's a 22 year old senior that makes $30k / month making ads for my activewear brand Haus.

TikTok Shop and Trybe are the lowest-risk, highest-upside opportunities ever created. No inventory, no LLC, no upfront cost. With TikTok Shop, you just post videos as an affiliate. With Trybe, you submit UGC ads to brands and they run them on Meta. If they do well, you get a % of the sales. 

But here's what most people miss: You might rip TTS and Trybe in college and by the time you finish you might not even need that degree.

You'll be making more than a doctor's salary by making content for a few hours a day.

By making ads for brands, you're not just making money, you're building the most valuable skill on earth - sales.

If you can sell products to strangers on the internet, you can sell anything to anyone. That skill alone is worth millions.

And naturally, by figuring out how to sell other people's products and by learning what makes consumers purchase, you may one day find yourself creating your own product or brand too.

A kid in my group started with zero followers and posted awkward videos for the first month. Made $200 his first week, $3K his second month, $15K by month three, $30k in month 4. 

The difference between him and everyone else complaining about "no opportunities"? He was willing to look stupid before he looked successful.

A LOT of people clowned him at school. Said it made him look stupid. He will likely be making their yearly salary every month by the end of this year. 

Most people would rather wait for the "perfect" business idea than start with something that works today.

TikTok Shop and Trybe works and it’s free. But it requires you to post your face online and maybe be awkward for a few weeks.

That's too high a price for most people. And that's why they stay broke.

content:
When the US military was searching for Osama Bin  Laden, the first thing they offered the locals was millions of dollars in US currency in exchange for information leading to his capture. 

Surprisingly, this did not work. Why? That’s not what the locals wanted. 

The locals could barely count to 100, so how would they understand the value of $25m in cash?

This is the same reason why most people fail at negotiation and convincing other to people to do things for them. They offer what THEY would want, not what the other person actually wants.

According to a tiktok video I saw of a Navy Seal, it wasn’t until they started to offer 50 goats as the reward that the locals wanted to share information. 

This same principal can be applied to business and life. 

You need to figure out what actually motivates people when negotiating with them.

I run the fastest growing activewear brand in the country and I’m constantly poaching top talent from my competitors and can almost never meet the comp they need, yet I always convince them to come over. How? I know how to figure out what truly motivates them, and most of the time, it’s not money.

(And it’s not goats either)

When you prioritize making other people money, beautiful things can happen

content:
How I’m using the tariffs to my benefit:

I run a men’s activewear brand and we source our products from China. Our industry will be one of the ones that are hurt the most.

But, there is another way to look at it.

I started my brand in a garage with my cousin with $9k.

In year 1 we did $630K
In year 2 we did $1.5M
We are projecting $7M in year 3

We also missed out on $1.1M in sales last year due to sold out SKUs

We are also profitable on the first customer acquisition. So, we don’t have a COGS problem, we have an out of stock problem. We can’t get our gear fast enough.

Since we are a small brand and have only just started our relationship with our manufacturer, we get placed at the back of their production line. We also just got payment terms for the first time ever.

They will likely lose a lot of business due to these tariffs. 

We plan on using this opportunity to strengthen our relationship with them. We are willing to stay in China and lose some $ on our orders if they can help us out by giving us more priority and a longer time frame to pay them back. 

These tariffs won’t last forever, and once they are gone, we will have created a much stronger foundation for our business moving forward.

There is always opportunity in chaos.

content:
If you are young and building anything, 
It can be extremely disheartening to see other young people your age drive around super cars and flex their watches while you put in every dollar and second of your time into this thing you truly believe in. 

You might even start to question yourself and ask “what am I doing wrong?”

Don’t be distracted by this kind of thing.

Odds are it’s either a sham, or they are selling an info product. 

Nothing against info products, but they are very different from actual concrete businesses.

Info products can provide lots of free time and short term cash since they require little upfront capital to start and typically have high margins. 

However, info products typically will not last longer than 2-4 years MAX and cannot be sold.

As a founder, you might spend 5+ years of your life, give up everything and have no financial guarantee of a return on your investment, but if it works out you could walk away with a massive check. And, even if it fails, you’ll still have a lot of experience to show for it. 

Not saying one is necessarily better than the other. Both have their benefits. Just don’t let the flashy object syndrome distract you.

content:
Heads up to my college friends graduating this spring

High paying career ≠ having a lot of money

If you don't like your career, you'll feel the need to buy back your happiness (ex: drinking and dumb purchases)

If you picked the career you loved, you'd  have less of a need to distract yourself

No more buying dumb things and drowning your sorrows every weekend

Some people work a shitty job to make a lot of money so that they don't have to work as much in the future

Others pick a job they love and they never feel like they are working at all

Also, if you love your job, you'll work harder and climb the ladder much faster, and you'll probably end up making much more longterm anyway
